nuggets.summary: In the first three years of building Indix, Sanjay's team rebuilt their technical architecture roughly every six months. The cause wasn't poor engineering discipline but a systematic underestimate of scale: they kept misjudging how much data they would need to store, how much memory the analytics would require, and how large their AWS bills would grow. The lesson for a founder building a data-heavy or infrastructure-heavy product is to expect early scale estimates to be wrong by a wide margin, and to budget for architecture churn as a normal cost of the first few years rather than a sign something is broken.

About a year before this interview, Indix killed a product line that represented all of its revenue at the time. The decision came from paying attention to qualitative pain signals from engineers and salespeople, not from the revenue numbers themselves, since the product was still generating the company's entire income. The harder and more important part wasn't recognizing the product was wrong (that was fairly easy once the pain was visible); it was that they refused to kill it until they had spent six months finding the replacement, because killing the only revenue source without a next thing to point resources at would have killed the company instead.

To catch when the company is building the wrong thing before it shows up in revenue, Sanjay's team runs an anonymous employee pulse-survey tool called TinyPulse, asking staff directly whether they're happy. He calls the underlying signal 'flow' — a proxy for whether engineers and salespeople feel the work is moving at velocity and mattering to customers. Because responses are anonymous, people report problems honestly, which gave the team an early warning sign before they killed their main product.

Against the common instinct to validate a startup idea with people who like you, Sanjay argues that only complete strangers who would actually write a check give useful feedback, because friends and acquaintances give encouragement instead of honest signal. As a concrete data point, when raising his seed round he pitched 18 people and 17 passed — which he treats not as discouraging but as a legitimate, informative result, since the value of the exercise is in the rejection rate itself, not in avoiding it.

Sanjay's explicit recommendation for early-stage founders is to raise a funding round once a year in the first few years — not primarily to get the runway, but because the act of pitching forces you to sharpen your thinking, and the volume of rejection you'll face is itself the mechanism that pushes you toward pitching the right thing. Indix followed this exactly: they raised every year for the first four years, and only after that did the gap between rounds stretch to two years, which he reads as evidence the pitch (and the underlying business) had finally found its footing.

Sanjay describes the common founder narrative — that an idea springs into being and then simply grows — as a myth. In his experience the process is subtractive rather than additive: you start with a rough, oversized block and chip away at it, the way a sculptor works stone. His own path illustrates this literally: he started with 'search engines don't work well outside the US/UK,' narrowed to 'a search engine for numbers,' narrowed further to 'a search engine for prices,' and only after about a year and a half arrived at the real, much larger opportunity — a product catalog for every product on the planet. The implication for founders is to expect the real idea to emerge from removing wrong framings, not from expanding a single initial insight.

Reflecting on 19 years at Microsoft versus 5 years running his own startup, Sanjay draws a distinction between building a career and building a character: a career is learning to navigate an existing system (in his case, a large company), while a character is learning to deal with your own fears, insecurities, and flaws when there's no system to lean on. He frames the startup years as having cost him some of the reflexive confidence he had at Microsoft, but as having given him something Microsoft never did — self-knowledge under pressure — reframing 'losing confidence' as a trade rather than a pure loss.

When evaluating whether a co-founder or senior hire can be trusted, Sanjay doesn't rely on agreement about ideas (he and his closest co-founder disagree often). Instead he probes for a shared underlying value system through abstract conversations — for example, one co-founder's strong belief in radical transparency (publishing everyone's salary) — and looks for independent, non-work evidence of grit and reliability, such as the fact that co-founder had run 150 miles across the Sahara Desert in seven days. The logic is that values alignment and demonstrated toughness predict whether someone shows up under pressure, which matters more than whether they're 'right' about any given decision.

To avoid drifting off course while heads-down in execution, Sanjay's executive team holds a formal strategy session every three months whose sole purpose is to check whether the company is still pointed in the right direction — separate from normal operating reviews. He credits the discipline of a fixed, short cadence (rather than checking in only when something feels wrong) with catching misdirection early, contrasting it with founders who go six months to a year before realizing they've drifted.

Sanjay says the hardest part of running the company isn't managing the team or facing customers in person — it's the moment he's alone reading bad news, such as an email from a customer cutting their budget. His developed technique is to deliberately not react in that moment: he calls it 'ignoring the reaction,' consciously delaying his emotional response and the mental cascade it triggers (renewal risk, fundraising risk, who has to be let go) rather than acting on the first-order panic, and returning to the decision later once that reaction has passed.

Sanjay's method for correcting his own emotional distortion after a setback is to describe the same situation to two other people who weren't involved, on the premise that they will almost always read it more favorably than he does in the moment — and, in his experience, they're usually right. He treats staying silent about a setback as actively costly, since isolation lets his own worst-case interpretation run unchecked; talking to his wife and a co-founder, and separately sharing Ben Horowitz's essay 'The Struggle' with his leadership team, functions as a deliberate outside-view check on his own read of a situation.

Rather than treating the 13.5-hour time difference and physical distance between his US and Chennai teams as a management liability, Sanjay treats it as the thing that forced him to actually trust his people, since he has no way to monitor day-to-day work across that gap. He explicitly separates trust from proximity: a team sitting in the next office that you don't trust is just as broken as a distant one, so distance isn't the root problem — the discipline of trusting without oversight is, and distance simply removes the option of avoiding that discipline.
